big: "Which index fund is best?" has no single answer, because an index fund is only as good a fit as the index inside it. Pick the list first, then the fund that copies it most cheaply and tightly.

lines: Which index fund is best? Just give me one.
One question first: best for what? Nifty 50, Nifty Next 50 and Nifty 500 behave very differently. Watch.

alt: Three lines for the Nifty 50, Nifty Next 50 and Nifty 500 over ten made-up years with the deepest fall of each
caps: Made-up paths. The Nifty 50 holds the 50 biggest companies. Next 50 holds the next 50 in size.
The Nifty 500 spreads across 500 companies, so it also holds mid and small ones.
Bigger swings in the Next 50. The Nifty 50 is the calmest of the three here.
Deepest falls here: Nifty 50 -14%, Nifty 500 -17%, Next 50 -24%. Pick the index to suit the goal.

alt: Bars comparing two funds on the same index by cost, tracking difference and size
caps: Now fix the index. Fund P and Fund Q both copy the Nifty 50. These numbers are examples.
Fund Q has the lower cost: 15 basis points against 30 for Fund P.
But Fund P trails the index by 35 basis points a year, and Q by 40. P tracks closer.
P is also much bigger. What you earn is the index minus the gap, so P leaves a little more.

title: Checks, and false shortcuts
stops: Choose the index to fit the goal first
Compare tracking difference on the same index
alt: A shield with true and false rules for picking an index fund
caps: First the index, to fit the goal. Then compare expense ratio and tracking difference on that index.
For ETFs, check size and trading volume. Look at how long the fund has existed.
The lowest fee on its own is not the test, and the three indices are not interchangeable.

q: Rohan sees that the Nifty Next 50 gave more than the Nifty 50 last year and wants a fund on it. In the made-up decade the Next 50's deepest fall was about 24% against 14% for the Nifty 50. What should be settled first?
opts: Which fund house is biggest, as it fixes how the index swings
Whether the larger falls fit his goal and his own nerves
Whether last year's return will repeat, to show the better index
Whether the fund has the lowest expense ratio, whatever the index
why: The house does not change the index's swings. Whatever fund he picks will behave like the Next 50.
The index sets the ride. A fall of about 24% is a different experience from 14%, so fit comes before fee.
One good year is no promise. Chasing it is how people end up with an index that does not suit them.
Cost matters but comes second. The index is chosen first, because indices differ more than funds do.

q: Two Nifty 50 funds: P has expense 0.30%, tracking difference 0.35% and ₹8,000 crore of assets. Q has expense 0.15%, tracking difference 0.40% and ₹300 crore. Which should Meena prefer?
opts: Fund Q, since the lower expense ratio always wins here
Either one, since the same index means the same return
Neither, since any fund below ₹10,000 crore is unsafe
Fund P, since it trails the index less and is bigger
why: The expense ratio is part of the gap, not all. Q trails by more in practice, so its lower fee did not help.
The same index does not give the same return. The gaps differ, and over years that adds up.
No size cut-off like that exists. Size is one check among several, not a pass mark.
She earns index minus the gap. P trails by 0.35% against 0.40%, and its size suggests it is well held.

q: An ETF on a Nifty index holds ₹20 crore and trades about ₹3 lakh a day. What risk should Rohan weigh before buying ₹5 lakh of it?
opts: Higher index returns, since small ETFs earn more
No risk at all, since an ETF always trades at NAV
A wide spread and a poor price when selling
Extra tax on each trade, since it is a small ETF
why: Size has no link with the return of the index. A small ETF earns the index return less costs, like any other.
An ETF trades at market price, which can differ from NAV. In a thin ETF the gap can be large.
Small size and thin volume can mean a wide spread. A ₹5 lakh order is large against ₹3 lakh a day.
Tax does not depend on the size of the ETF. The risk here is the trading price, not the tax.

q: A fund launched three months ago on the Nifty 50 has the lowest expense ratio of any. What is the sound view?
opts: Its record is too short to judge, so prefer an older fund
Buy it now, since the lowest fee always means the best result
Avoid it for ever, since any new fund is bad by definition
Judge it on three months of returns, since they show tracking
why: Tracking difference needs a year or more of data. A fee alone says little about how well it copies the index.
A low fee is one point. A new fund can have poor tracking or low assets, so the fee does not settle it.
New funds can turn out well. The point is to wait for evidence, not to rule them out for ever.
Three months is too short. Short periods are noisy and say little about tracking.

pts: Choose the index first. Nifty 50, Next 50 and Nifty 500 behave very differently.
Then compare expense ratio and tracking difference among funds on the same index.
Check size, trading volume (for ETFs) and how long the fund has existed.
